newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Peres tells Mideast leaders to tango toward peace.
newsitem.headline: Peres tells Mideast leaders to tango toward peace.

text.p: Former Israeli Prime Minister Shimon Peres, on a visit to Argentina, advised his successor Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat on Monday to copy the tango if they wanted peace.
"In Argentina, the home of tango, you know that to dance well you have to close your eyes and the romance begins. Peace is a romantic process, it's not mechanical," he said.
Peres said on arriving in Buenos Aires he believed the peace process was "in crisis, but not in danger ... There is still time for us to find a way out of this crisis."

Nobel laureate Peres was ousted last year by Netanyahu, who was meeting U.S. President Bill Clinton on Monday and was expected to refuse again to scrap plans to build Jewish housing in Arab East Jerusalem that have enraged Palestinians and led to the current crisis.
Opposition leader Peres was among thousands of Israelis at a peace rally in Tel Aviv on Saturday appealing for an immediate return to talks that have been stalled for about a month.

Netanyahu is mulling a possible unity government to achieve consensus for peace. Peres, asked whether he would take Labour into such an alliance, said there would be "just one condition -- that the peace process continues."

"We have no interest in participating in the Netanyahu government just for the sake of being in government. We would only be ready to form a unity government if peace was the objective, because peace is our aim," Peres told reporters.

The Labour leader was in Argentina to receive honorary doctorates and meet the leaders of a country that is home to one of the world's largest Jewish communities. Jews in Argentina have suffered two major attacks recently -- a bomb at the Israeli Embassy in 1992 that killed 29 people and one at the AMIA Jewish community centre in 1994 that killed 86.

Peres, who is scheduled to meet Argentine President Carlos Menem on Wednesday, expressed regret that Argentine police still have not caught the culprits but rejected out of hand one Argentine judge's recent speculation that the embassy bombing could have been the work of Jewish hardliners.
"We completely rule out the idea that Jews could have carried it out," Peres said, adding that Israel had "no doubt that it originated in Iran."
